Two source landmarks round out the layer. The top-level sklearn/__init__.py re-exports the public surface by hand. And for exploring rather than consuming, all_estimators in sklearn/utils/discovery.py, L22 enumerates every estimator class in the package, filterable by kind.

The fit/transform Contract and Estimator Chaining

Open sklearn/base.py and you find the whole philosophy in one file. BaseEstimator does not know anything about learning; it knows about configuration. Its get_params at L248 inspects the estimator’s own __init__ signature and returns exactly the keyword arguments it was born with. This one decision — hyperparameters only in the constructor, data only in fit — is what makes every downstream tool possible: you can serialize, compare, and rebuild any estimator from its parameter dictionary, with no hidden state.

clone at L46 is the enforcement arm of that decision. It takes an estimator, pulls its params, and constructs a brand-new unfitted twin, raising an error if any constructor default was tampered with. Cross-validation and grid search lean on this constantly: nothing ever reuses a fitted model across folds, so there is no leakage by construction. Mixins then layer on capabilities: ClassifierMixin, L561 contributes a score method and tags, RegressorMixin, L631 and ClusterMixin, L719 do the same for their families, and is_classifier at L1245 is the runtime test the rest of the library uses to branch on estimator kind.

The transformer half of the contract is fit returning self and transform turning data into data. TransformerMixin composes them into fit_transform, and since fit hands back the object itself, calls chain naturally: scaler.fit(X).transform(X) reads like a sentence. This contract is what estimator chaining is built on — scikit-learn ships a helper that stitches a list of transformers to a final estimator into one composite object, and that helper contains no magic beyond calling fit_transform down the line and fit at the end. The composition exists so cross-validation treats the entire chain as one unit: the scaler learns its statistics inside each fold, never from held-out data. Doing it by hand — fit the scaler on the training fold, transform both folds, fit the model — gives exactly the same semantics.

The newest contract extension is metadata routing, and its layout teaches how the project evolves without breaking old imports. BaseEstimator inherits _MetadataRequester from sklearn/utils/_metadata_requests.py, L1665, where MetadataRequest, L633 records which keywords an estimator is willing to receive and MetadataRouter, L980 lets meta-estimators declare where those keywords should flow. The file you might import by name, sklearn/utils/metadata_routing.py, is now a thin re-export shim — a live example of the project treating its import surface as a public promise.

Under the Hood: Cython Kernels and Parallel Dispatch

The detail view: Python estimators on top, the validation and parallelism utilities in the middle, and the Cython kernels doing the heavy lifting underneath.

The detail diagram above is really a story about two languages. Python owns the parts where flexibility matters — API, validation, orchestration — and Cython owns the parts where the inner loop would otherwise drown in interpreter overhead. The cleanest example is a single decision tree. DecisionTreeClassifier in sklearn/tree/_classes.py is a friendly Python class, but its fit immediately hands control to sklearn/tree/_tree.pyx, a depth-first builder that recurses over nodes in compiled code. Each node asks sklearn/tree/_splitter.pyx to hunt for the best feature and threshold, and the splitter scores every candidate using the Gini and entropy kernels in sklearn/tree/_criterion.pyx. None of that allocates a Python object per candidate.

The same pattern repeats across the library once you know to look for it. K-means is a Python orchestrator in sklearn/cluster/_kmeans.py wrapped around a Lloyd iteration kernel in sklearn/cluster/_k_means_lloyd.pyx, which does the assignment and center-update passes on contiguous arrays. The penalized linear models use a coordinate-descent inner loop in sklearn/linear_model/_cd_fast.pyx, and the gradient boosting family keeps its regression-tree kernels in sklearn/ensemble/_gradient_boosting.pyx. The names end in .pyx, and finding them in the tree is the fastest way to locate the true hot spots of any subsystem.

Parallelism gets the same treatment. sklearn/utils/parallel.py wraps joblib — its Parallel at L41 subclasses joblib’s own so that configuration and warning filters travel with the task into worker processes, and delayed at L95 is the marker that turns a call into a schedulable unit. The forest code shows the canonical usage: _parallel_build_trees at L135 is the per-tree job, and the BaseForest class at L188 fans it out across processes or threads depending on n_jobs. A subtle detail worth respect: the same module pins thread counts on BLAS libraries during parallel regions, so nested parallelism never thrashes your cores.

Model Selection and Metrics

The selection subsystem is where the estimator contract pays its biggest dividends, because sweeping configurations is only safe if cloning is airtight. The splitters in sklearn/model_selection/_split.py — train_test_split at L2771 for the one-shot case, KFold, L437 for the general rotation — produce index pairs and nothing else — no data, no models — which is why the same splitter objects can be reused across experiments safely.

GridSearchCV in sklearn/model_selection/_search.py then becomes almost simple to read: for every combination of parameters and every fold, clone the base estimator, fit it on the fold’s training slice, and score it on the validation slice. The scoring step is itself pluggable through string names — get_scorer at sklearn/metrics/_scorer.py, L478 resolves "accuracy" or "roc_auc" into a callable, and check_scoring at L947 validates the pairing between estimator and scorer so a regressor is never judged by classification metrics. Underneath, the metrics modules like the one holding accuracy_score at L357 do the actual arithmetic, sharing the same multiclass bookkeeping utilities so results are consistent no matter which entry point you use.

Reading this subsystem end to end changes how you use it. Refitting the best estimator on the full data after the search is not a bolted-on convenience — it falls out of the clone discipline: every fitted candidate is disposable by design, and the search remembers only the winning configuration. That is the kind of property worth copying into your own experiment code.

Honest Limits

For all its polish, scikit-learn is explicit about what it is not. It is not a deep learning framework — there are no GPUs in the core, no autograd, and no batched training of neural networks; that is PyTorch’s territory, and the two cooperate well in mixed workflows. It is not a text or sequence modeling stack; for pretrained language models you will reach for Transformers and treat scikit-learn as the layer around it for classical metrics and calibrations. And it is not a data management system: the bundled datasets are toys and small classics, and anything real belongs in something like Datasets upstream, loaded into NumPy or sparse matrices before fit ever sees it.

Deployment has its own boundary. Fitted scikit-learn models serialize happily with joblib, but serving them outside Python means converting them — the ONNX route is the standard answer, and tools like skl2onnx translate most estimator families to a portable graph that ONNX Runtime executes at native speed. The conversion layer is community-maintained rather than core, so exotic custom estimators are exactly where you should budget testing time.

None of these limits diminish the central achievement. In a field where interfaces churn yearly, one library has kept the same two-verb vocabulary — fit and transform — stable enough that code from a decade ago still runs and reads naturally. Read sklearn/base.py for the contract, sklearn/utils/validation.py for the discipline, and one .pyx kernel for the performance engineering, and you will have absorbed design lessons that outlast any single framework.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of scikit-learn: the fit/transform contract, estimator chaining, Cython kernels, and the model selection machinery, with two architecture diagrams.

entry.title: spaCy Source Tour: How the Industrial NLP Library Fits Together

link.title: spaCy Source Tour: How the Industrial NLP Library Fits Together

entry.content:
spaCy needs little introduction. It is the industrial-strength natural language processing library from Explosion, written in a deliberate mix of Python and Cython, and it has become the default choice when you need tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, named entity recognition, or text classification that actually runs fast in production. Unlike scikit-learn, which treats text as a bag of features for classical estimators, spaCy is opinionated about document structure: every text becomes a Doc object, and a configured stack of processing components annotates that object in a fixed order. If you have read our Tokenizers post, you saw how byte-level BPE breaks text into subwords; spaCy answers a different question — how to turn raw text into linguistically structured objects a model can learn from and an application can act on.

The source is worth reading because the performance story is not a wrapper around something else. Files like spacy/tokenizer.pyx, spacy/tokens/doc.pyx, and spacy/ml/parser_model.pyx are Cython that compiles down to C, and the whole design follows a simple discipline: keep the hot path in compact structs, keep orchestration in thin Python. At the same time, the neural side is built on Thinc, Explosion’s own functional deep-learning library, so model wiring is declared in config files and resolved through a registry rather than hand-coded class hierarchies. That combination — Cython data structures plus registry-driven Thinc models — is what makes spaCy feel different from both classic ML libraries and the Transformers ecosystem.

In this tour we walk the repository the way a request flows through it: the Language engine that owns everything, the tokenizer that produces the Doc, the Doc object model that every component shares, the Thinc models underneath tagging, parsing and entity recognition, and finally the training loop that ties them together. Two diagrams anchor the tour — a compact overview and a deeper detail map — and every symbol we mention is linked to the real source on GitHub so you can follow along in the tree.

The spaCy overview: one Language engine owns the tokenizer and component stack, Thinc models do the learning, and every path ends at the shared Doc object.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • [Language](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/language.py#L138) is the nlp object. [add_pipe](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/language.py#L768) registers a processing component by name, [__call__](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/language.py#L1020) runs the whole stack over a text, and [make_doc](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/language.py#L1114) hands off to the tokenizer.
  • The [Tokenizer](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/tokenizer.pyx#L25) is pure Cython with no neural component at all. Its [__call__](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/tokenizer.pyx#L152) applies prefix, infix, and suffix rules plus an optional exception table; a batched [pipe](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/tokenizer.pyx#L212) exists for bulk work.
  • [Vocab](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/vocab.pyx#L46) centralizes string storage, lexeme metadata, and vector tables so that one nlp instance shares a single hash-to-string map across all documents.
  • [Doc](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/tokens/doc.pyx#L130) is the container every component reads and writes: the tokenizer fills it, taggers and parsers annotate it, and [set_ents](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/tokens/doc.pyx#L800) turns character-level predictions into entity spans; [noun_chunks](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/tokens/doc.pyx#L888) exposes one of the derived views.
  • [Tok2Vec](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/tok2vec.py#L102) builds the shared token encoder — [MultiHashEmbed](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/tok2vec.py#L122) for hashed embeddings, then a [MaxoutWindowEncoder](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/tok2vec.py#L275) or [BiLSTMEncoder](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/tok2vec.py#L328) for context.
  • [ParserStepModel](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/parser_model.pyx#L236) is the transition-based step predictor shared by the dependency parser and the entity recognizer — one Cython model, two grammars of actions.
  • The rule-based side lives in [Matcher](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/matcher/matcher.pyx#L32): [add](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/matcher/matcher.pyx#L79) registers token patterns with optional [on_match](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/matcher/matcher.pyx#L214) callbacks, no training data required.
  • [train](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/training/loop.py#L35) drives optimization by calling nlp.update, and [train_while_improving](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/training/loop.py#L153) adds early stopping on a dev set.
  • [load_model](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/util.py#L492) in spacy/util.py resolves a package name, directory, or shortcut into a fully assembled Language object.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting started is deliberately short:

pip install spacy
python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm

Then in Python:

import spacy
nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
doc = nlp("PyShine ships fast text analytics.")
print([t.text for t in doc])
print([(e.text, e.label_) for e in doc.ents])

Three things happen inside that innocent spacy.load. First, [load_model](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/util.py#L492) locates the installed package and reads its config.cfg, a serialized description of the tokenizer settings and every component with its factory and hyperparameters. Second, that config is resolved through the registry — the same mechanism you will meet on the Thinc side — so each component is constructed by a registered factory function rather than a hardcoded import. Third, the returned Language object wires the components in the declared order; at runtime nlp(text) tokenizes once and then lets each component annotate the shared Doc in sequence.

This config-first design is why spaCy models are inspectable. Call nlp.analyze_pipes() and the library reports, per component, which attributes it sets and requires — the implementation is [analyze_pipes](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/pipe_analysis.py#L81), a small module that earns its place by catching ordering mistakes like a lemmatizer placed before a tagger. The same discipline powers training: [init_nlp](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/training/initialize.py#L35) builds a fresh Language from config, and only afterwards does data touch the model. Nothing about your first model was special-cased; it was assembled from the same parts you would assemble for a custom one.

The Doc Object Model: One Array, Many Views

The deepest design decision in spaCy is the Doc. Its constructor at [__init__](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/tokens/doc.pyx#L202) allocates flat C arrays — one per annotation field — sized to the token count. A [Token](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/tokens/token.pyx#L44) is not a Python object holding its own data; it is a lightweight view with an index into those arrays, created on access. A [Span](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/tokens/span.pyx#L24) is the same trick for a token range. Iterating a document therefore costs no object churn: you are reading typed views over memory the document already owns.

This is also why the tokenizer can be so fast. Because Doc storage is preallocated and the string interning lives in [Vocab](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/vocab.pyx#L46), splitting a sentence is just pointer arithmetic and hash lookups. The vocabulary pairs each string with a [Lexeme](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/lexeme.pyx#L43) — cached flags like is_alpha, is_stop, and language-specific attributes — while [Morphology](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/morphology.pyx#L14) compresses feature bundles into dense slot tables and [Lookups](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/lookups.py#L162) holds data tables such as lemma dictionaries loaded from the language data directory.

The practical consequence: annotations are decoupled from algorithms. Entity boundaries set via [set_ents](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/tokens/doc.pyx#L800), dependency arcs, morphological features, and custom extension attributes all live as parallel arrays on the same document, so any component can consume any other component’s output without a special interface. It also makes serialization uniform — a Doc and its annotations survive a round trip through DocBin unchanged, which is exactly what the training data machinery relies on.

Extension attributes deserve a mention too, because they show how far the view idea is pushed. User code can attach its own per-token, per-span, or per-document values through the underscore module, and those custom attributes ride along in serialization like built-in ones. Retokenization — merging multi-token expressions into one or splitting a token in two — is implemented as a surgical array splice on the same document, so a rule-based matcher and a merge step can cooperate without rebuilding anything. Both facilities exist precisely because the document is a data structure rather than a bag of Python objects.

The detail map: Doc storage and its views on one side, the Thinc model zoo and the transition-based step model in the middle, matchers, training and rendering utilities around them.

Under the Hood: Thinc Models and Transition Systems

Every trainable component in spaCy is a thin shell around a Thinc Model. The shared encoder pattern shows up first: [build_Tok2Vec_model](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/tok2vec.py#L102) composes hashed embedding tables with a context encoder, and downstream components subscribe to its output with the listener mechanism — see [tok2vec_listener_v1](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/tok2vec.py#L31), which lets a component receive gradients from another component’s encoder instead of keeping a private copy. The tagger is the minimal example: [build_tagger_model](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/tagger.py#L9) wires encoder output to a softmax over tag classes. Text classification varies the head instead of the encoder — [build_simple_cnn_text_classifier](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/textcat.py#L46) pools token vectors, while [build_textcat_parametric_attention_v1](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/textcat.py#L218) learns how much each token should matter.

Structure prediction goes through transition systems. [build_tb_parser_model](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/parser.py#L13) assembles the stacked architecture, and the actual state machine lives in Cython: [ParserStepModel](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/parser_model.pyx#L236) scores the next action for a batch of partial parses, with [precompute_hiddens](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/parser_model.pyx#L368) hoisting the expensive encoder pass out of the per-step loop. The entity recognizer reuses this machinery with a different action set — which is why tagging, parsing, and NER all feel consistent once you have read one of them.

More specialized heads follow the same recipe. Span categorization builds ragged span representations in [build_spancat_model](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/spancat.py#L46) and scores candidates against configurable length ranges. Entity linking adds retrieval to the mix: [build_nel_encoder](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/entity_linker.py#L30) encodes mention context and [load_kb](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/ml/models/entity_linker.py#L93) pulls the knowledge-base side, so disambiguation becomes a similarity problem against candidate identifiers.

Training, Batching, and Evaluation

Training data is expressed as Example pairs. The Cython class at [Example](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/training/example.pyx#L78) holds a predicted Doc and a reference Doc plus an alignment between them, so losses can be computed token-aligned even when tokenization differs. Converters bring external corpora into this format — [conllu_to_docs](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/training/converters/conllu_to_docs.py#L11) handles CoNLL-U treebanks, which is the bridge from academic datasets to spaCy training, and the rest of the Datasets world plugs in through the same entry points.

The loop itself is refreshingly small. [train](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/training/loop.py#L35) alternates shuffling, batching, nlp.update, and evaluation; [minibatch_by_padded_size](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/training/batchers.py#L95) groups examples of similar padded length so tensor work is not wasted on padding. Evaluation funnels through the [Scorer](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/scorer.py#L111), which aggregates token-level, span-level, and text-level metrics into one report, and [train_while_improving](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/training/loop.py#L153) stops when the dev score plateaus. For debugging outputs visually, the renderers in spacy/displacy/render.py — [SpanRenderer](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/displacy/render.py#L52), [DependencyRenderer](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/displacy/render.py#L291), and [EntityRenderer](https://github.com/explosion/spaCy/blob/master/spacy/displacy/render.py#L504) — turn the same Doc annotations into SVG and HTML.

Honest Limits

The small pretrained models that most people start with trade accuracy for speed; for competitive numbers you move to transformer-based weights, at a real cost in memory and latency. Tokenization is rule-based per language: excellent for well-formed text, but domain-specific text (social media, code, historical orthography) often needs custom exceptions or a different tokenizer altogether, as our earlier tokenizer survey shows.

Architecturally, the component stack is sequential and unidirectional — a component sees the document only after earlier components have finished, and sharing beyond the tok2vec-listener mechanism is limited, so genuinely interactive multi-task inference is awkward to express. Training requires gold data in the Example format; there is no first-class path from raw unlabeled text to a custom component short of pretraining tricks. Entity linking is powerful but presumes you can build and host a knowledge base. Finally, the Cython layer means you should not expect to edit a .pyx file and rerun — a C compiler toolchain and the build steps from the repository are required, which raises the bar for casual contribution compared to pure-Python libraries. None of these are hidden; they are the visible trade-offs of a library optimized to be fast and predictable in production, and knowing where the C ends and the Python begins is the key to extending it confidently.

Read this way, the repository is less a black box than a layered argument: compact Cython structures where speed matters, a registry-driven model layer where flexibility matters, and a small orchestration core that keeps both honest.
entry.summary: A guided tour through the spaCy source tree: the Language engine, the Cython Doc object model, Thinc neural models, rule-based matching, and the training loop.

entry.title: Stable-Baselines3 Source Tour: How PyTorch Reinforcement Learning Is Wired

link.title: Stable-Baselines3 Source Tour: How PyTorch Reinforcement Learning Is Wired

entry.content:
Reinforcement learning has a reputation for being hard to implement correctly. Small details — how advantage estimates are normalized, when a target network copies weights, how entropy is folded into the objective — decide whether an agent learns or silently diverges. Stable-Baselines3 from DLR-RM is the reference-quality answer to that problem: a faithful PyTorch reimplementation of the classic Baselines algorithms, built on Gymnasium environments, with readable code and consistent structure across every learner it ships. If you have ever trained PPO, SAC, DQN, or A2C and wondered what actually happens between model.learn() and a saved zip file, this tour is for you.

What makes this codebase worth reading is not just the algorithms — it is the shared scaffolding underneath them. One abstract base class defines the contract for all learners; two loop templates cover the on-policy and off-policy families; a small set of buffers, policy factories, and vectorized environment wrappers fills in the rest. Because the scaffolding is shared, reading one algorithm teaches you the shape of all of them. That consistency is also why the library has become the de facto baseline in academic RL papers: when a paper says “SB3 default hyperparameters,” reviewers know exactly what that means.

This post walks the source top-down. We start with a high-level architecture diagram, zoom into a detail diagram that maps every major module, trace a first training run line by line, and finish with an honest look at where the library’s abstractions bend. Everything referenced below links to a real symbol at a real line number in the master branch, so you can follow along in your editor.

The overview graph shows how two loop templates and five algorithm classes hang off one abstract base, with buffers, policies, vectorized environments, and callbacks as shared services.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • BaseAlgorithm, L67 is the abstract parent of every learner: it owns the environment reference, device selection, seeding, logging, and the save/load machinery that all children inherit.
  • OnPolicyAlgorithm, L21 implements the rollout loop — collect a batch of fresh experience, train on it, throw the data away, repeat.
  • OffPolicyAlgorithm, L27 implements the replay loop — store every transition forever (up to capacity), sample mini-batches, and interleave environment steps with gradient updates.
  • PPO, L18 and A2C, L16 are the on-policy children; most of their files are just objective functions and hyperparameters.
  • SAC, L19 and DQN, L19 are the off-policy children, adding entropy regularization and target networks respectively.
  • RolloutBuffer, L343 and ReplayBuffer, L158 implement the two storage disciplines — fixed-size batches versus a large ring of transitions.
  • ActorCriticPolicy, L416 is the default neural policy: a feature extractor plus actor and value heads, reused by PPO and A2C.
  • VecEnv, L50 defines the vectorized environment interface — the reason a single learn() call can step eight or sixteen simulators in lockstep.
  • BaseCallback, L31 provides the hook points that let you inject evaluation, checkpointing, or custom logic without touching algorithm code.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting running takes three lines beyond the install. The idiomatic first program looks like this:

import gymnasium as gym
from stable_baselines3 import PPO
from stable_baselines3.common.env_util import make_vec_env

env = make_vec_env("CartPole-v1", n_envs=8)
model = PPO("MlpPolicy", env, verbose=1)
model.learn(total_timesteps=100_000)
model.save("ppo_cartpole")

Each line maps to a specific module. make_vec_env, L40 builds a vectorized environment, wrapping each copy in a Monitor that records episode rewards and lengths. The PPO constructor walks up the inheritance chain to BaseAlgorithm._setup_model, which resolves the policy string "MlpPolicy" into a real network, creates the rollout buffer, and configures the learning-rate schedule — the library expresses schedules as a simple Schedule, L29 callable that maps a progress fraction to a float.

The call to model.learn() lands at learn, L512 in the base class, which normalizes arguments, wires callbacks, and delegates to the concrete subclass. From there the rollout loop takes over: collect_rollouts runs the policy against the vectorized environment until the buffer holds n_steps * n_envs transitions, then train() performs the clipped-surrogate updates. Finally save, L819 bundles parameters and metadata into a zip artifact, and load, L643 reconstructs the agent from it. The round trip is deliberately boring — no pickle of whole objects, just data you can inspect.

One habit worth copying from the docs early: evaluate deterministically, and do it automatically with EvalCallback, L342, which runs evaluate_policy, L12 every eval_freq steps, keeps the best checkpoint, and can stop training early when rewards plateau. The callback API is small — _on_training_start, _on_step, _on_rollout_end — but it covers essentially every integration need without forking the library.

Reproducibility gets first-class treatment too. set_random_seed threads a seed through PyTorch, NumPy, and the environment stack at construction time, and the base class picks the device automatically — CPU, GPU, or Apple silicon via MPS — while exposing it as a constructor argument. The logger module is the quiet hero here: every algorithm reports episode reward, loss terms, and exploration statistics through the same key-value interface, so swapping verbose=1 console output for a TensorBoard dashboard is a one-line TensorBoardCallback away. When a run misbehaves, you can diff two experiments’ logged keys rather than guessing from stdout noise.

On-Policy vs Off-Policy: Two Loops, One Base Class

The single most instructive contrast in the codebase is between the two loop templates. The on-policy loop lives in OnPolicyAlgorithm.learn, and its heart is collect_rollouts, L162: step every environment, store observations, actions, rewards, dones, and log-probabilities into the RolloutBuffer, and let the policy’s value function bootstrap the terminal state. When the buffer fills, train, L270 computes advantages with generalized advantage estimation and runs several epochs of minibatch gradient descent — for PPO that means the famous clipped ratio between new and old policy probabilities. The data is then dead weight: the next rollout starts from a fresh buffer, because the policy that generated it no longer exists.

The off-policy loop inverts the economics. OffPolicyAlgorithm.learn, L324 keeps a persistent ReplayBuffer of buffer_size transitions and, each step, performs gradient_steps updates sampled uniformly from history. Its own collect_rollouts, L526 also handles exploration strategies and warmup: until learning_starts transitions exist, actions come from the exploration noise rather than the policy. DQN plugs epsilon-greedy and target-network syncing into train, L190; SAC replaces exploration noise with an entropy-regularized stochastic policy tuned automatically in train, L205; TD3 adds twin critics and delayed policy updates at train, L160.

The practical consequence: on-policy algorithms spend most of their wall-clock time collecting environment steps and are sample-inefficient but stable; off-policy algorithms squeeze many gradient steps out of each environment interaction and excel when simulation is expensive. The base class keeps both loops honest — progress reporting, callback dispatch, logging cadence, and evaluation hooks behave identically whether you are training PPO or SAC, because the loop templates share that code.

Inside the Detail Diagram

The detail graph expands each overview box into real modules: policy factories and their network pieces, the buffer family including hindsight replay, concrete vectorized environments, and the tooling belt of callbacks, evaluation, and plotting.

Zooming in, three subsystems deserve attention. First, the policy stack: BasePolicy, L280 is the root class, and concrete families specialize it — SACPolicy, L181 for squashed Gaussian actors, TD3Policy, L86 for deterministic actors with twin critics (which DDPG reuses verbatim), and DQNPolicy, L88 for Q-networks. Under them sit shared neural building blocks in torch_layers (the NatureCNN for Atari-style pixels, MlpExtractor for actor-critic heads) and a clean probability layer in distributions that handles discrete, Gaussian, and state-dependent-noise action spaces uniformly.

Second, the environment stack. DummyVecEnv, L15 steps simulators sequentially in-process and is the right default; SubprocVecEnv, L79 moves each environment into its own process when Python-side simulation cost dominates. Wrappers compose freely: VecNormalize, L15 maintains running statistics to normalize observations and rewards, and because it is a wrapper, it composes with either backend. The Monitor wrapper records per-episode statistics to csv so that plot_results can turn training logs into learning curves later.

Third, the buffer family. Beyond the two core buffers, HerReplayBuffer, L15 implements hindsight experience replay for goal-conditioned tasks — after an episode ends, failed trajectories are relabeled so the achieved goal becomes the intended one, turning sparse-reward failures into dense learning signal. The type-safe sample structures live in type_aliases, which is also where the Schedule alias used for learning rates and clip ranges is defined.

Honest Limits

Stable-Baselines3 is deliberately a library of proven classics, not a catalog of the frontier. You will not find model-based RL, distributional methods like Rainbow, population-based training, or the latest sequence-modeling agents here — the maintainers explicitly prioritize correctness, documentation, and consistency over algorithm count. If your research needs something exotic, expect to write it yourself, though the loop templates make that less painful than it sounds: a new on-policy method is usually a subclass that overrides train().

The abstraction also has a cost. Everything is tuned for the vectorized-environment regime, so single-environment training takes a configuration detour, and custom observation wrappers must respect the Gymnasium API precisely or you will hit shape errors deep inside buffer indexing. Recurrent policies exist but are more involved than the feedforward default, and large-scale distributed training is out of scope — the library assumes one machine, one learner, many simulators. For RLHF-scale infrastructure where hundreds of workers feed a central learner, projects like OpenRLHF live in a different weight class, even though they still lean on SB3-style algorithmic conventions.

Documentation and testing, to be fair, are where this project shines rather than struggles. Every algorithm ships with the same benchmark plots, docstring hyperparameter references, and type hints. The main practical pitfall is subtler: default hyperparameters are tuned per environment suite, so PPO defaults that ace Atari can underperform on continuous control unless you adjust n_steps, batch_size, and the entropy coefficient. Reading the source — especially the annotated train() implementations — is the fastest way to build the intuition for which knob does what.

Where to Go Next

A good reading order inside the repo: start with base_class.py for the lifecycle, then on_policy_algorithm.py next to buffers.py to see the rollout loop and its storage as one picture, then ppo.py as the most complete on-policy objective, and finish with sac.py plus sac/policies.py to watch entropy regularization thread through an off-policy learner. Along the way you will notice how much heavy lifting the Gymnasium integration does — the observation and action space objects drive buffer shapes, network input sizes, and distribution choices automatically, which is why respecting the Gymnasium API contract matters so much.

If this tour was useful, the natural companions on this blog are the Gymnasium environment tour, the PyTorch internals walkthrough for the tensor-level machinery underneath, and scikit-learn for the classical-ML contrast in API design. And if your interest in RL is really about aligning large models, OpenRLHF shows where the same on-policy loop ideas scale to PPO-based post-training of LLMs — same concepts, very different plumbing.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the DLR-RM/stable-baselines3 codebase: BaseAlgorithm, the on-policy and off-policy training loops, buffers, policies, vectorized environments, and the hooks that make PPO, SAC, and DQN tick.

entry.title: TorchAO Source Tour: How PyTorch’s Quantization Library Actually Works

link.title: TorchAO Source Tour: How PyTorch’s Quantization Library Actually Works

entry.content:
If you have ever run a quantized LLM through plain PyTorch and wondered where the speed-up actually comes from, TorchAO is the answer hiding in plain sight. TorchAO (the torchao pip package, developed in the pytorch/ao repository) is PyTorch’s native quantization and sparsity library: it takes your ordinary nn.Linear layers, swaps their weights for compressed tensor representations, and dispatches the math to hand-written low-bit kernels. Unlike standalone quantization tools, everything it does is expressed in the language of the framework itself — tensor subclasses, dispatch, and torch.compile — which is exactly why its source is worth reading.

The second reason to study this codebase is architectural. TorchAO is not one big monolith; it is a thin public API on top of three cooperating layers: a recipe layer (dataclass configs that users touch), a transform layer (a registry that maps recipes to module surgery), and a tensor layer (subclasses like Int8Tensor and Float8Tensor that own the quantized data layout and their own kernels). Once you see how a config flows from quantize_() down to a .cpp file, you can predict where any new feature will land — and you can read llm-compressor or vLLM integration notes with far less guesswork.

This post is a source tour of the repository at main, walking the tree from the public API down to the metal. The two diagrams below were generated directly from the real file tree, and every symbol and line anchor in the text was verified against the current source.

The TorchAO overview: user recipes enter through quantize_(), get dispatched by a small handler registry into tensor subclasses, and terminate in native int8, int4, and float8 kernels.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • quantize_() — the eager entry point in quant_api.py, L292. It walks your model, filters for linear modules, and applies one recipe per module in place. Everything else in the library is downstream of this function.
  • AOBaseConfig — the base class for all recipes at config.py, L27. Every public config dataclasses from it, which is what lets TorchAO serialize recipes to JSON and round-trip them through checkpoints.
  • register_quantize_module_handler — the registry decorator in transform_module.py, L19. Each recipe type maps to exactly one transform function; quantize_() looks the handler up by config type and calls it.
  • Int8Tensor — the dynamic int8 activation + int8 weight subclass in [int8tensor.py, L59](https://github.com/pytorch/ao/blob/main/torchao/quantization/quantize/workflows/int8/int8_tensor.py#L59). Its linear override at L266 intercepts F.linear and routes to integer matmul kernels.
  • Int4Tensor — the weight-only int4 subclass in [int4tensor.py, L57](https://github.com/pytorch/ao/blob/main/torchao/quantization/quantize/workflows/int4/int4_tensor.py#L57). Its linear path at L190 now dispatches to fused rowwise int4 kernels instead of the older tinygemm op.
  • NF4Tensor — the 4-bit NormalFloat representation in [nf4tensor.py, L580](https://github.com/pytorch/ao/blob/main/torchao/quantization/quantize/workflows/nf4/nf4_tensor.py#L580), the same quantization family that made QLoRA popular, implemented as a first-class tensor.
  • Float8Tensor — the fp8 inference tensor in [float8tensor.py, L84](https://github.com/pytorch/ao/blob/main/torchao/quantization/quantize/workflows/float8/float8_tensor.py#L84), for Hopper-class GPUs where 8-bit floating point beats integer formats.
  • quantize_affine — the numeric primitive in quant_primitives.py, L364. Scale/zero-point computation, requantization, and dequantization all reduce to this layer, with dequantize_affine as its mirror at L749.
  • register_custom_op — the bridge in ops.py, L45. Ops like torchao::da8w4_linear_cpu declared here connect the Python tensor layer to the C++ and CUDA sources under torchao/csrc/.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is deliberately boring: pip install torchao. The package builds shipped extension modules against a compatible PyTorch, and the top-level torchao/__init__.py checks versions at import time — if your torch is older than 2.11, it warns and skips loading the .so files rather than crashing, so the pure-Python APIs still work. On Apple Silicon there is an optional extra path: the torchao/experimental/ tree exposes Metal-backed low-bit kernels for MPS devices.

Your first quantized model is three lines:

import torch.nn as nn
from torchao import quantize_
from torchao.quantization.quant_api import Int4WeightOnlyConfig

model = MyModel().cuda()
quantize_(model, Int4WeightOnlyConfig(group_size=32))

What actually happens next is the interesting part. quantize_() uses the default filter to visit every nn.Linear, resolves the handler registered for Int4WeightOnlyConfig, and lets that handler replace each module’s weight with an Int4Tensor. The quantization itself respects a granularity object — PerRow at granularity.py, L79 or PerGroup at L58 — which maps down to the block_size argument of quantize_affine. After the swap, model.linear.weight is no longer a plain tensor; it is a dispatch table. Every subsequent forward pass hits the subclass’s __torch_dispatch__ implementations, so no model code changes at all.

Pick recipes by hardware. Int8DynamicActivationInt8WeightConfig (defined at quant_api.py, L852) is the CPU and torch.compile workhorse; Int8WeightOnlyConfig at L746 halves memory with near-zero accuracy loss; Int8StaticActivationInt8WeightConfig at L962 uses calibration-time scales for fastest integer math; and Float8DynamicActivationFloat8WeightConfig at L1156 targets fp8-capable GPUs. On the export side, the PT2E flow — prepare_pt2e at quantize_pt2e.py, L63 followed by convert_pt2e at L439 — produces a graph of quantized ops that ExecuTorch can deploy to phones and embedded targets.

CPU deployments deserve a special mention because TorchAO treats them as first-class. The Int8DynamicActivationIntxWeightConfig recipe at quant_api.py, L368 pairs dynamically quantized 8-bit activations with flexible 1-to-8-bit weights, and its CPU execution path bottoms out in the C++ da8w4_linear.cpp kernel rather than a Python fallback. If your architecture hides linear layers inside 1x1 convolutions — common in diffusion and vision models — the swap_conv2d_1x1_to_linear helper at quant_api.py, L236 rewrites those modules first so the recipes can see them. For maximum compression on memory-bound CPU inference, IntxWeightOnlyConfig at L1408 packs weights down to sub-byte widths and relies on lookup-table-style kernels to decode them on the fly.

The detailed view: recipe dataclasses carry packing formats and granularity into the transform registry, tensor subclasses own dispatch, and a thin custom-op bridge hands work to C++ and CUDA kernels.

Under the Hood: Recipes to Kernels

The transform chain is worth appreciating because it is so small. transform_module.py is a single dictionary plus a decorator; the intelligence lives in the handlers defined next to their recipes in quant_api.py. A handler receives the module and the config, calls the appropriate quantize-tensor function, and returns a new module whose weight is a subclass instance. There is no code generation and no global state — which is why recipes compose cleanly and why adding a new format rarely touches more than two files.

The same discipline shows up in the numeric plumbing. Every recipe ultimately calls choose_qparams_affine at quant_primitives.py, L1254 to derive scales and zero points for a block of weights, then hands the results to the tensor constructor. Storage layout is declared, not guessed: the PackingFormat enum at packing_format.py, L12 gives every subclass a stable identifier for how its bytes are arranged, which is what makes checkpoint round-tripping and cross-device transfers inspectable instead of magical.

Each tensor subclass is where layout meets execution. Int8Tensor stores quantized data plus scales and owns every aten op it cares about: linear, slice, embedding, and friends. Its kernel module defines safe_int_mm at kernels.py, L18 — a guarded integer matmul that pads dimensions to satisfy cuBLAS requirements — and _int_scaled_matmul_cpu at L79, which picks a u8s8 path when AVX512-VNNI is available and an s8s8 path on AMX hardware. The int4 side exposes Int4PackingFormat at [int4packing_format.py, L12](https://github.com/pytorch/ao/blob/main/torchao/quantization/quantize/workflows/int4/int4_packing_format.py#L12) with plain, preshuffled, and tile-packed layouts, and Int4ChooseQParamsAlgorithm at [int4choose_qparams_algorithm.py, L12](https://github.com/pytorch/ao/blob/main/torchao/quantization/quantize/workflows/int4/int4_choose_qparams_algorithm.py#L12) lets you trade a slower HQQ calibration for better rounding. The float8 recipes grow a KernelPreference field — the enum at kernel_preference.py, L17 — so a config can request Torch-native or specialized kernels and let the tensor resolve it at dispatch time.

Beneath the Python sits torchao/csrc/, organized by target: CPU shared kernels such as the 8-bit-activation x-bit-weight linear used by ExecuTorch deployments, an aten_kernels directory holding da8w4_linear.cpp for dynamic-activation int4-weight CPU inference, AArch64 NEON-dot headers for phone-class hardware, and CUDA sources for microscaling fp8 plus 2:4 semi-structured sparsity via CUTLASS on Hopper. The fp8 sparse tensor — Float8Sparse2x4_1DData1DMetadataTensor at [float8sparse_2x4_1d_data_1d_metadata_tensor.py, L42](https://github.com/pytorch/ao/blob/main/torchao/quantization/quantize/workflows/float8/float8_sparse_2x4_1d_data_1d_metadata_tensor.py#L42) — shows the pattern end to end: the Python class declares a custom fp8_sparse_mm op, ops.py gives it a schema, and the CUDA file implements it.

Training is a sibling rather than an afterthought. The torchao/float8/ package converts a model for fp8 training with convert_to_float8_training at float8_linear_utils.py, L86, swapping eligible layers for Float8Linear at float8_linear.py, L206 with per-tensor or rowwise scaling strategies. QAT users get QATConfig at qat/api.py, L43, which inserts FakeQuantizedLinear at qat/linear.py, L42 modules so weights learn under the same numerics they will be quantized to later. Even optimizer memory is covered: OptimState8bit at subclass_8bit.py, L40 stores Adam moments as quantized tensors, extending the same TorchAOBaseTensor base at utils.py, L721 that the inference subclasses use.

Honest Limits

TorchAO is PyTorch-coupled by design, and that cuts both ways. The shipped binaries track specific torch releases; run an older torch and the extension load silently degrades to a warning, meaning your “quantized” model may fall back to dequantize-then-float math that is slower than the original. Kernel coverage is also hardware-shaped: the fast int4 rowwise paths assume modern NVIDIA GPUs or specific ARM CPUs, the fp8 and CUTLASS sparse paths need Hopper-class cards, and the fancy MPS Metal kernels are opt-in through the experimental API. On unsupported targets you get correct-but-unremarkable performance, not the benchmark numbers.

Accuracy is a per-model negotiation, not a guarantee. Weight-only int8 and group-wise int4 are broadly safe for LLMs, but dynamic-activation int8, fp8, and anything with coarse group sizes need numerical checking against your own eval — the repo’s testing utilities, including benchmark_model at utils.py, L75, help, but they do not replace a proper eval harness. The PT2E flow additionally requires an export-compatible model, and its prepare/convert contract has churned across PyTorch versions, so pin your versions. Finally, the repository moves fast: sparsity has migrated into prototype and float8 subtrees, the old linear_activation_quantized_tensor.py files are gone in favor of the workflows layout, and int4 kernels now route through the mslk ops. Any source tour — including this one — has a shelf life, so anchor to a commit, not to main.

Where TorchAO Sits in the Stack

Compared with llm-compressor, which produces compressed checkpoints for serving engines, or vLLM, which consumes them, TorchAO keeps everything inside eager PyTorch and torch.compile — you quantize a live module, not a file. That makes it the natural choice when you want quantization to survive fine-tuning, export cleanly through ExecuTorch, or compose with PyTorch training utilities without leaving the ecosystem. Read the three layers in order — recipe, transform, tensor — and the whole codebase opens up.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the torchao source tree: quantize_ recipes, tensor subclasses, packing formats, and the C++ and CUDA kernels that make low-bit inference fast.
